Advanced composite materials like graphite epoxy and Kevlar epoxy have significantly different electrical properties compared to traditional metals like aluminum.
Graphite epoxy has moderate electrical conductivity, allowing it to conduct lightning currents, while Kevlar epoxy is an electrical insulator.
Graphite epoxy can be used for power ground returns up to about 10 A, but Kevlar epoxy cannot be used in this way due to its dielectric nature.
Bonding composites to metal can be achieved through techniques like using tapered bolts or electroless plating the composite with nickel prior to bonding.
Composite materials have lower thermal conductivity and different thermal expansion coefficients compared to metals, which can lead to integration challenges.
Graphite epoxy requires a sacrificial metal layer at lightning attachment points to prevent damage, while Kevlar epoxy requires comprehensive metal shielding to protect the aircraft.
Graphite epoxy provides a reasonable ground plane for VHF and higher frequency antennas, but not at lower HF frequencies. Kevlar epoxy provides no usable ground plane at any frequency of interest.
The reduced conductivity and shielding effectiveness of composite materials can lead to increased electromagnetic interference and coupling issues that need to be addressed.
The use of low-conductivity composite materials can reduce the radar cross section of the aircraft, which may be desirable for certain applications but requires careful design considerations.
Helicopters have unique considerations such as rotary wings, large openings, fixed landing gear, and nap-of-the-earth navigation that need to be addressed when using composite materials.
System-level tradeoff studies are crucial to balance the advantages of composite materials with the challenges they introduce and to develop holistic solutions.
The Advanced Composite Airframe Program (ACAP) aims to achieve a 22% weight saving and a 17% cost saving by using advanced composite materials.
Over 80 reports and conference papers on the effects of advanced composite materials on avionics systems have been collected and summarized in this report.
The report discusses the impact of composite materials on various avionics systems and subsystems, including power ground returns, bonding, antennas, EMI/EMC, and radar cross section.
Possible solutions and approaches to the challenges posed by composite materials are presented, including the importance of system-level tradeoff studies.
